doc.title: Sam Most interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: What he thinks about when improvising
summary: Practiced material becomes subconscious; he thinks of chord names and lyrical melody.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: You know, you asked Lester Young a question about what do you think about when you’re improvising and he gave you that answer. What if I ask you the same question. Is it possible to put it into words?

I don’t know. I think it’s hard for me to explain it myself. I try to get the emotional thing of course. I think it’s a matter of all your experiences that come through too, but I think a lot of the things that you practice and everything comes into your improvisation, you know the technical thing. And sometimes it becomes maybe subconscious, the different exercises you practice, like [scats] so that goes with certain chords or certain scales and everything. And of course when you’re playing you don’t always think well I’m playing [scats] but from knowing these things and having it — just like classical training I guess — having this facility you are able to manipulate the chords or the harmonies instantaneously with some of these things that you have maybe under your fingers in your
mind. And so all that comes into play and sometimes some thinking of the chords while I’m playing say a standard.
Sometimes you’re thinking of the chords but not always?

Not always, or else just the name of the chord see? I’m B flat now. And then automatically I think of melodies. I remember having an interview a long time — Metronome, Down Beat, saying like I like the lyrical quality. Like as if you are singing. Pretty melodies like [scats] something that makes sense and I always liked that. And that’s what I sort of think about. So say if you know you’re in B flat, then you know the intervals and what you can do. And you make up a melody right on the spot.
And that’s more or less, I don’t know if you can get any deeper in it, but that’s the idea.
Yeah. I know what you’re saying.
It’s a hard thing to put into words, and sometimes it just depends on the tune too. It seems like sometimes you have to think harder about the chords because of the particular changes in that song.

Right, right. Other times it kind of flows naturally, like what is it, two, six, two one. I mean one, six, two, five or that type of thing. You just don’t think about it because you hear it and then say I know this [scats] it’s easy.
